items.title: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The US economy grew at its fastest pace in a year in the third quarter, shrugging off higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East as consumers maintained robust spending and businesses doubled down on investment in AI.

The better-than-expected increase in gross domestic product last quarter reported by the Commerce Department on Thursday was in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and deterioration in consumer sentiment.

The advance GDP report was published less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress. Economists said the strong growth, together with other data on Thursday showing inflation accelerating and broadening out in September, bolstered the argument for the Federal Reserve to raise interest rates in December.

The US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."

"The consequences of an economy at full employment in addition to a historic capital expenditures expansion are on vivid display," said Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM. "If the Fed is looking for more information on why they should act to restore price stability they can find it inside a slate of robust spending ... stratospheric private non-residential investment and sizzling inflation data."

Gross domestic product increased at a 3.4% annualized rate last quarter, the quickest since the third quarter of 2025, the Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis said in its first estimate of third-quarter GDP. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast GDP advancing at a 3.2% pace.

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Fed officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. Stocks on Wall Street were trading lower. The dollar slipped against a basket of currencies. US Treasury yields fell.

Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, increased at a 3.8% rate in the July-September period, matching the second quarter's pace. It was largely driven by services, including healthcare, visits to restaurants and bars as well as hotel and motel stays.

There was a pullback in spending on goods like motor vehicles and household furniture. Higher-income households, whose wealth has been boosted by AI-related strength in the stock market, are driving much of the spending.

Historically low layoffs and moderate hiring are also helping other households to sustain spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation. Households are also saving less and dipping into their nest eggs. The saving rate fell to 4.1% from 4.4% in the second quarter. It fell to 3.8% in September.

"Growth isn't enough to give American families economic security," said Kyle Moore, chief economist at the Century Foundation. "Most of that growth has been lopsided, focused on the AI buildout. Wages for the typical worker still aren't keeping up with increasing prices."

Business spending on equipment surged at a 20.9% rate, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020. That added 1.16 percentage points to GDP growth, the most in six years. Information processing equipment, mainly computers and peripheral equipment, made up the bulk of the contribution.

Business spending on intellectual property products grew at an 8.4% rate, adding just under half a percentage point to GDP growth, mostly coming from software and research and development. Robust consumer and business spending were both sated with imports, which are a drag in the calculation of GDP.

Imports increased at a 19.7% rate, the quickest since the first quarter of 2025, when businesses were front-loading orders to avoid higher costs from Trump's sweeping tariffs.

LARGE DRAG FROM IMPORTS

Imports last quarter sliced off 2.64 percentage points from GDP growth, which was more than offset by the strength in consumer and business spending as well as a 1.61 percentage point contribution from the rebuilding of inventories, which had been drawn down for five straight quarters.

Government spending increased at a 5.3% rate amid a sharp rebound in federal government outlays, both defense and nondefense. Rising mortgage rates because of the Middle East conflict pushed residential investment back into contraction last quarter. Higher borrowing costs have overshadowed a moderation in house prices, weighing on demand for housing.

A measure of domestic demand, which excludes inventories, trade and government, accelerated at a 4.9% rate, the strongest since the second quarter of 2021. Final sales to private domestic purchasers grew at a 4.6% rate in the second quarter. Economists viewed the current pace of demand as unsustainable.

While inflation subsided last quarter as the cost of energy eased, price pressures picked up at the end of the third quarter.

The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index increased 0.5% in September after rising 0.3% in August, the BEA said in a separate report. In the 12 months through September, PCE inflation advanced 3.6% after rising 3.4% in August. It is one of the measures tracked by the Fed for its 2% inflation target. Rising inflation, with average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, left economists anticipating a slowdown in economic growth by year end.

Income at the disposal of households after accounting for inflation and taxes dropped 0.3% last month after being flat in August. Inflation-adjusted consumer spending was unchanged in September after rising 0.5% in August, putting consumption on a weaker growth path heading into the fourth quarter.

Economists also expected some moderation on AI-related spending as investors are focusing on the rising costs of long-term projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending.

"An economy increasingly supported by stock-market wealth and large technology projects also faces risks if share prices retreat or investment plans disappoint," said Sung Won Sohn, a finance and economics professor at Loyola Marymount University.

items.title: US weekly jobless claims hover near 57-year lows
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The number of Americans filing new claims for unemployment benefits hovered near 57-year lows last week amid labor market resilience.

Initial claims for state unemployment benefits fell 1,000 to a seasonally adjusted 194,000 for the week ended October 24, the Labor Department said on Thursday. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast 199,000 claims for the latest week.

Claims have stayed mostly below 200,000 since mid-September and are within striking distance of the 189,000 level touched in mid-July, which was the lowest reading since 1969.

Economists view the labor market as remaining in a "low-hire, low-fire" state. They said strong profits as domestic demand remains resilient were keeping layoffs near historic lows. But the ongoing US-Israeli war with Iran was making employers hesitant to increase headcount, economists said.

The claims report showed the number of people receiving unemployment benefits after an initial week of aid, a proxy for hiring, dropped 21,000 to a seasonally adjusted 1.701 million during the week ended October 17.

The so-called continuing claims covered the week during which the government surveyed households for October's unemployment rate. The jobless rate was at 4.2% in September, and could remain steady or even edge down this month as a Conference Board survey on Tuesday showed consumers more optimistic about the labor market in October.

A reduction in the labor force amid the Trump administration's immigration crackdown is a key factor in keeping the unemployment rate low. The Federal Reserve on Wednesday left its benchmark overnight interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."

Economists expect the US central bank to raise rates in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh acknowledged the labor market stability, telling reporters that "on the employment side of the Fed's dual mandate, conditions are quite positive."

items.title: US couple's retirement dream in ruins after residential cruise scrapped in Cambodia
items.content_html:
SIHANOUKVILLE, Cambodia, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Americans Lynn and Paul Montoya sold their house and cars in Wyoming so they could afford to buy a $179,000 cabin on the residential cruise ship Villa Vie Odyssey, plus roughly $6,000 a month in fees, to spend their retirement sailing the globe.

Their dream lasted 17 months on the ship before its operator abruptly announced this week that soaring fuel prices were forcing it to suspend operations. The company, Villa Vie Residences, informed the Montoyas and some 200 other passengers they had to disembark from the Odyssey at a port in Cambodia, along with pets and any personal items they could carry from their homes at sea.

"We really hadn't travelled that much out of the United States until probably a few months before we boarded the ship... and we just saw it as a great opportunity to be able to see the world," Paul told Reuters.

Uncertainty over the ship's future is more than just a travel hiccup for those who spent tens of thousands of dollars hoping to make it their home for years to come.

"They've run out of money," Paul said. "That's why they couldn't buy fuel. They've even had difficulties paying the crew on the ship, which even makes it more difficult. So we're really not expecting any money back."

Villa Vie did not respond to emailed questions or phone calls. In a statement on Tuesday, it said it was seeking to restructure and recapitalize, but no deals had been finalised.

"That work is ongoing, and no outcome is assured," the company said, and added it was working to support those affected.

SIGNS MONEY WAS RUNNING OUT

As the war with Iran dragged on and fuel prices rose, Paul said residents noticed growing problems aboard the Odyssey. The company asked passengers to contribute more, and asked residents to provide a loan for fuel, he said.

"And then when we got to Cambodia, absolutely no internet," he said. "And the food quality began to deteriorate about three months ago, and we knew that the company was running out of money at that time."

The Montoyas said they now planned to live off the money they had budgeted for the monthly fees and spend some time in Malaysia.

Lynn said they would miss the community aboard the ship more than the lost money.

"It's hard to lose that money, but I also look at it as, we've had 17 months of going to the most amazing places and meeting the most amazing people," she said.

items.title: Alaska dispute threatening to complicate fight for US Senate control
items.content_html:
ROCK HILL, South Carolina, Oct 29 (Reuters) - Alaska’s Republican governor has ordered a state investigation of allegations in a New York Times report that Democrats recruited spoiler candidates in the state’s US Senate race, raising the prospect of a messy fight over a contest that could determine Senate control in next Tuesday's midterm elections.

Alaska is one of about 10 highly competitive races that will decide control of the Senate, where Republicans hold a 53-47 majority. Democrats need a net gain of four seats, and a post-election dispute in Alaska could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks.

Governor Mike Dunleavy said on Wednesday that the probe would examine whether any laws were broken, posting on X that "the evidence will determine what happens next," hours after the Times reported that aides to Democratic candidate Mary Peltola worked to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan.

President Donald Trump told reporters on Thursday, "It's hard to believe that she could even be allowed to run. Frankly, I don't know how you can allow somebody like that to run. It's so unfair.”

Trump for years has sowed doubts about the fairness of US elections and even prior to the Times report had pushed the Justice Department to file a lawsuit seeking to preemptively block Alaska from certifying Peltola, a former congresswoman, if she were to win the election.

The Times reported on Wednesday that Peltola aides worked with campaign lawyers and staff at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to recruit two candidates who could siphon votes from the incumbent Republican Sullivan, including a retired teacher also named Dan Sullivan who is on the ballot. Peltola’s former campaign manager, Elisa Rios, who was fired in August, told the Times that Peltola was aware of the effort.

Peltola’s campaign said it “has no involvement with either Sullivan campaign.” The DSCC also denied involvement and accused Republicans of propping up candidates of their own in other races.

'CULTURE OF DECEPTION'

House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, on Thursday lambasted what he called the "crazy tactics" of Democrats in Alaska, saying in an interview with Fox News that "we hope it doesn't confuse voters, but that's exactly what the Democrats tried to do here. They got caught red-handed."

US Senator Lisa Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, called for Peltola to be honest.

"Recruiting candidates to manipulate the field and influence voting outcomes is simply wrong. Alaskans deserve the honest truth from Mary and her campaign — what has been revealed is a pattern of lies and coverups and a culture of deception that belongs nowhere in our elections or among our elected officials," she posted on X.

Jessica Levinson, a professor who specializes in election law at Loyola Law School in Los Angeles, said that as long as Daniel J. Sullivan, the challenger to the incumbent, didn’t conceal financial support, his campaign likely didn’t break any laws and political parties are allowed to mislead the public.

Policing such behavior would open the door to the government investigating why candidates choose to run and why voters support them, she said. "To the extent that people are uncomfortable with two Sullivans, I would offer you're probably going to be uncomfortable with a really high level of government intrusion into our elections as well."

Rex VanMiddlesworth, an executive board member of Keep Our Republic, a nonpartisan group that works to build trust in US elections, said on a call with reporters that nothing would bar the second Sullivan from the ballot or disqualify Peltola. He called the Justice Department’s lawsuit “frivolous even by current DOJ standards,” saying it cites no provision of law.

TRUMP IN SOUTH CAROLINA, HARRIS IN GEORGIA

Trump held a rally in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday, his second visit in two weeks to a state where opinion polls show an unexpectedly close race between Republican Senator Darline Graham and Democrat Annie Andrews. A few protesters were escorted out as Trump spoke from the stage.

Speaking about the hotly contested Michigan Senate race, where progressive Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed holds a small lead in most polls over Republican Mike Rogers, Trump continued his identity-based attacks on El-Sayed, a Muslim, by saying at the rally that "if you're Black or if you're Jewish, and if you vote for Abdul, you're crazy."

With control of the Senate at stake, both parties are deploying their biggest names in the closing days of the campaign, with Trump stumping for Republicans and former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigning for Democrats in competitive races.

Harris stumped in Macon, Georgia, at a get-out-the-vote effort. Democrats are aiming to see Senator Jon Ossoff, who leads in polling, reelected, and hope that Keisha Lance Bottoms, locked in a tight race, can become the first woman elected as governor in the state.

Trump’s approval rating stood at 32% in a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday, near a record low, as Americans sour on the high cost of living and the war with Iran.

Some 41.4 million Americans had already voted as of Thursday morning, according to the University of Florida’s Election Lab. A total of 45.9 million voted early in the 2022 midterms.

items.title: US files lawsuit claiming Google wouldn't give employee new job following military leave
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 29 (Reuters) - The US filed a lawsuit accusing Google (GOOGL.O), opens new tab of failing to give an employee his old job back or find him a similar job after he took one year of military leave as a US Army reservist.

Thursday's lawsuit in Manhattan federal court is a rare instance of the US government suing a private employer for violating the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act of 1994 (USERRA), which protects the civilian employment of military personnel called to active duty.

According to the complaint, Mark Davisson spent 2-1/2 years before taking military leave as a Google key account executive, handling cloud services accounts for asset manager BlackRock (BLK.N), opens new tab and hedge fund Bridgewater Associates, and managing the US business of the former Credit Suisse.

Upon Davisson's return from leave in May 2023, Google allegedly refused to let him handle any customer accounts, depriving him of career advancement though he kept his pay and title.

EMPLOYEE FIRED AFTER FURTHER MILITARY LEAVE

The complaint said Google assigned Davisson in January 2024 to a cloud solutions position that also involved no management of customer accounts, and fired him seven months later as part of a broader workforce reduction and following another military leave.

Davisson, a Bronze Star and Meritorious Service Medal recipient, has a home in Charlotte, North Carolina, but lived and worked in Manhattan while Google employed him, the complaint said. Google's parent Alphabet is based in Mountain View, California.

"We disagree with the claims in this complaint," Google spokesman Atle Erlingsson said in an email. "Google takes compliance with employment laws, including USERRA, seriously and investigates allegations of workplace wrongdoing."

SUPPORT FROM TRUMP'S CIVIL RIGHTS CHIEF

The lawsuit was brought by the civil rights unit of the US Attorney's office in Manhattan, with backing from Assistant Attorney General Harmeet Dhillon, the Trump administration's top civil rights enforcer.

It seeks to recoup lost wages and benefits as well as additional damages for Davisson, and require Google to ensure a nondiscriminatory workplace including by improving USERRA training.

“Federal law ensures that our brave soldiers, who sacrifice so much to keep us safe, are not punished by employers when they return to the civilian workforce after completing their military service,” US Attorney Jamie McDonald in Manhattan said in a statement.

items.title: Judge says Trump bid to set aside California ballots would ‘wreak havoc’ on democracy
items.content_html:
Oct 28 (Reuters) - A US judge strongly rebuked the Trump administration on Wednesday by rejecting a request by the Justice Department to temporarily block California from counting mail ballots for the midterm elections from more than 20,000 registered voters the department alleges are likely noncitizens.

The decision marks the latest setback for President Donald Trump's effort to boost the federal government's role in elections ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party locked in a tight battle to retain control of both houses of Congress.

US District Judge David Carter issued the decision, opens new tab after a hearing on Tuesday in Los Angeles federal court over the Justice Department's request for a temporary restraining order barring officials from counting any ballots from the individuals it flagged.

The Justice Department's lawsuit, filed on October 15, was a rare intervention in the voting process weeks before an election and signaled the Trump administration's willingness to contest the midterm results in court.

"Never before in American history has the federal government, on the eve of an election, sought to coerce a state and local government to abandon their own Constitutional elections procedures and bend to the will of the Executive Branch," Carter wrote on Wednesday.

The judge, an appointee of Democratic President Bill Clinton, said the Justice Department's last-minute request to exclude over 20,000 ballots ran afoul of "longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections."

Carter warned that a ruling in the Trump administration's favor would "wreak havoc" and cause thousands of registered voters to "potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve."

"Eroded trust in our democracy is irreparable," Carter wrote. "Once a vote is segregated, lasting harm has occurred. If the Executive can discount votes and threaten an ongoing election due to unproven allegations, then our democracy is in danger."

The Justice Department swiftly appealed the decision to the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals.

"Every day, more ballots are processed by election officials," Justice Department lawyer Bill Essayli said in a statement. "This ongoing emergency disenfranchises American citizens through dilution."

California has said the state's safeguards against noncitizen voting are robust. It said the Justice Department's assertions relied on "suspect data" and that complying with its demands would risk disenfranchising eligible voters.

California is the most populous US state and a Democratic stronghold. It has more seats in the House of Representatives — 52 — than any other state.

Trump has made California a focal point of his sweeping immigration crackdown since returning to the White House, accusing it of undermining public safety through its "sanctuary state" policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

Trump has repeatedly insisted that states are not doing enough to stop voting by noncitizens, which he says is widespread despite multiple studies and state audits showing it is rare.

APPEALS COURT REJECTED EMERGENCY REQUEST

Carter ruled two days after a federal appeals court on Monday rejected an unusual emergency request by the Justice Department asking the appeals court to temporarily block California from counting the ballots before Carter had the chance to rule.

The Justice Department did not indicate how many of the more than 20,000 people it flagged in California had actually submitted a mail ballot.

It had argued that a restraining order was necessary to ensure that California did not impede prosecutors' ability to enforce a federal law that makes it illegal for noncitizens to vote in federal elections.

But Carter said the Justice Department never explained why counting ballots would impair any prosecutions under the law, as states are not required to help the federal government investigate and prosecute crimes.

Apart from California, the Trump administration has sought to intervene in elections in two states that are home to competitive races.

In Alaska, the Justice Department last week asked a judge to prevent certification of election results if the Republican incumbent senator loses by a slim margin, alleging that the presence of another candidate with a similar name on the ballot could confuse voters. Alaska has urged that the case be dismissed, arguing it has taken steps to distinguish the two candidates on the ballot.

In Washington state, the Justice Department on Monday sent a letter asking officials not to count any ballots received from 400 voters it said may not be citizens. Washington's top elections official said the timing of the request indicated it was intended to cast unfounded suspicion on election results.

California had 23 million registered voters as of December 2025, while Washington had 5 million registered voters as of 2024, state records show.

Voting rights activists have expressed concern that the federal government's methods for scrutinizing state voter lists to identify noncitizen voters risk wrongly flagging naturalized citizens for removal from the rolls.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US DOJ is inquiring about Nvidia's purchase of Hugging Face, sources say
items.content_html:
SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The US Department of Justice has made inquiries about how Nvidia’s (NVDA.O), opens new tab $12.93 billion deal to buy open-source platform Hugging Face would affect competition in artificial intelligence, at the same time as antitrust enforcers pursue their years-long investigation into the chip designer's conduct, two people familiar with the matter said.

The Justice Department's recent questioning covers Nvidia's acquisitions, investments, sales practices, and whether the chip designer has exerted pressure on its customers, the two people said. On Hugging Face, Justice Department officials have asked whether the deal would let Nvidia capture a fundamental distribution point for AI, the people said. The acquisition is expected to close in the first half of 2027, Nvidia has said, adding that Hugging Face would continue to support work with a range of chip, cloud and AI providers.

The department's questions around the Hugging Face deal and details of its continued pursuit of Nvidia's conduct more broadly are reported for the first time here. Nvidia has become a cornerstone of the tech economy and AI boom, backing major players such as Anthropic and OpenAI while spurring data center development globally so its chips can power AI's voracious computing needs.

Any action by the DOJ could ripple through the chip industry and challenge Nvidia's investing and acquisition strategy that has extended its influence in AI. Government investigations are not evidence of wrongdoing and do not necessarily result in lawsuits.

A DOJ spokesperson declined to comment on any matters before the department, citing longstanding policy. The spokesperson added, "This DOJ under President Trump’s leadership will continue to prioritize advancement of Super Intelligence for the betterment of the American people."

Nvidia declined to comment, and Hugging Face representatives did not respond to a request for comment.

The broad Nvidia examination started under former Democratic President Joe Biden and has continued under the administration of Republican President Donald Trump, during which time Nvidia has been the most valuable company in the world and a singular force in AI. There is no indication that Trump has any involvement, and the probe may not result in any Justice Department action.

As part of the probe, the DOJ has examined Nvidia’s acquisition of SchedMD, one of the people said. The December 2025 purchase sparked worries among AI specialists about their access to SchedMD's open-source software, which helps run supercomputers relevant to national security. Nvidia has vowed to continue open access and support.

NVIDIA AND TRUMP

Nvidia has the biggest share of the market for AI chips, which power the likes of ChatGPT, Anthropic's Claude and similar tools. A host of startups and chip-design companies have challenged its dominance.

Competitors Broadcom (AVGO.O), opens new tab and Alphabet's (GOOGL.O), opens new tab Google design processors together, seeking to beat Nvidia hardware with chips purpose-built for specific tasks and AI software. Advanced Micro Devices (AMD.O), opens new tab has said it can produce technically superior hardware and has struck billion-dollar deals with several AI labs and cloud computing operators.

Nvidia's market position has nonetheless made it an industry force and helped CEO Jensen Huang develop a relationship with Trump, who has touted American AI. Huang and Trump have made frequent appearances together, with the CEO joining the president's diplomatic trip to China. Trump, who has disclosed owning Nvidia stock, separately awarded Huang the National Medal of Science for advancing AI hardware.

Trump critics have previously accused the administration of political intervention at the DOJ, which the administration has disputed. Such intervention is traditionally out of the ordinary.

Staff-led investigations at the DOJ often take years and can stretch from one administration to the next. In addition, the DOJ routinely seeks input from companies when evaluating proposed mergers. "It would be inappropriate for the Department to conduct a merger investigation under the guise of a conduct investigation," the DOJ spokesperson said.

SCRUTINY OF OTHER NVIDIA DEALS

The DOJ has scrutinized Nvidia's conduct following other transactions, including its 2025 deal to license technology from chip startup Groq and hire its engineers, the people said. Officials have explored whether Nvidia unfairly offered larger allocations of AI chips if customers purchased its networking equipment and Groq processors, raising questions about whether Nvidia used its dominant product to push into a newer market, the people said.

Nvidia declined to comment, and Groq did not respond to a request for comment.

The DOJ has also looked at Nvidia's acquisition of Run:ai, which makes software that helps AI chips run more efficiently, the people said.

The department's questions about the proposed Hugging Face acquisition include identifying how Nvidia might use the AI platform to harm rivals in the AI market, and whether Nvidia could use the newly acquired business to gain leverage, the people said.

Officials are also asking questions about Hugging Face's competitors, said the people.

items.title: Democrats recruited spoilers in Alaska Senate race, NYT says
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Democrats recruited potential spoilers in Alaska's US Senate race, the New York Times reported, opens new tab on Wednesday.

Aides to Mary Peltola, the Senate Democratic nominee, worked with the campaign's lawyers and senior staff at Senate Democrats’ campaign arm to recruit two candidates who are on the ballot and could siphon votes from incumbent Republican US Senator Dan Sullivan, according to the Times.

Alaska's ranked-choice ballot will feature Sullivan, Peltola, a retired teacher whose name is also Dan Sullivan and a longshot candidate named Gerald Heikes, who has run for governor and the US House of Representatives multiple times. Heikes replaced Democrat David Leslie after the progressive candidate was urged to withdraw.

Elisa Rios, Peltola's former campaign manager, told the newspaper that Peltola was aware of the effort but not directly involved. Representatives for Peltola and Elias Law Group, whose attorneys represent Peltola, did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee denied involvement.

"Republicans have a long history of recruiting and propping up candidates in an attempt to boost their own campaigns – including recruiting a prisoner with a New York address to run against Mary Peltola and spending nearly half a million dollars to secure a spot on the ballot in Alaska for an Arizona resident in the Senate race this cycle,” said Monica Robinson, a spokesperson for Senate Democrats' campaign arm.

Republican super PACs during the primary sought to boost a third-party candidate who lives in Arizona. A Democratic super PAC did the same for Heikes and another Republican candidate.

The US Department of Justice preemptively filed suit in federal court last week to block certification of Alaska's election results if Sullivan narrowly loses his reelection bid. Lawyers for Peltola's campaign have asked the judge to dismiss the Trump administration's lawsuit.

Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy, a Republican, said he was calling for a state investigation into whether any laws were broken, writing on X overnight: "The evidence will determine what happens next."

Republicans hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate, meaning Democrats would need to pick up four seats in the November 3 midterm elections to win control of the chamber.

Alaska, a state Republican President Donald Trump won by 13 percentage points in 2024, is one of several battlegrounds that will determine which party holds the Senate for the final two years of Trump's presidency.

items.title: Trump expands hunt for noncitizen voters with broad subpoena campaign before midterms
items.content_html:
Oct 28 - The Trump administration has issued more than 100 subpoenas demanding records on tens of thousands of voters in at least 13 states, part of an escalating effort ahead of next week’s midterm elections to uncover evidence of unlawful voting by people who aren’t US citizens.

Most of the subpoenas documented by Reuters were issued to state and local election officials in the past three months, though some date to the start of the year. Many were previously unreported, revealing a federal effort to identify potential noncitizen voters that is broader than publicly known. It is illegal for noncitizens to vote in US federal elections. Legal experts say the records could be used to contest results in close midterm races, despite scant evidence that voting by noncitizens is widespread.

Reuters identified the subpoenas through public-records requests and interviews with local and state officials. Many were issued in Democratic strongholds, including Minneapolis, Philadelphia, Los Angeles and other California cities. But they also reach into Republican-leaning states with competitive races, including Texas, Kansas and Georgia.

At least 49 of the subpoenas were issued under the authority of grand juries, indicating they are tied to criminal investigations and making them generally harder to challenge in court than administrative subpoenas issued directly by federal agencies.

The White House says noncitizen voting is a significant problem that warrants the sweeping federal effort to identify and prosecute such cases, including through the deployment of hundreds of federal law enforcement agents. It has vowed to keep the effort a top priority. “The Trump administration is sending a clear message that anyone who illegally votes in our elections will be held accountable,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement to Reuters. “Only Americans should be electing America’s leaders.”

Multiple studies and a Reuters analysis have found that noncitizen voting is exceedingly rare.

The subpoenas are one piece of an expansive campaign targeting noncitizen voting. Armed Homeland Security agents have questioned residents in several states about their immigration status and voting, while the Justice Department has sued 30 states that refused to provide voter rolls containing sensitive personal information such as driver’s license numbers and partial Social Security numbers. A federal judge largely halted Homeland Security’s field operations in nine states on October 21, and courts have ruled against the Justice Department in every voter-roll case so far. Many of those cases remain under appeal.

The subpoenas issued by the Justice Department and Homeland Security offer another way to obtain the same voter information, which legal experts say could figure in disputes over midterm election results. Elections are administered primarily by the states, with the federal government playing a limited role. Under most state laws, only losing candidates or voters can challenge election results, but the Justice Department could still take legal action to delay or block certification of winners.

Heavily Democratic California offers a glimpse of how such a fight could unfold. Its congressional seats could decide who controls the US House of Representatives. The Justice Department alleged this month that more than 20,000 “likely” noncitizens in California had received mail ballots and demanded any ballots cast by them not be counted until their citizenship was verified. California officials refused and called the list unreliable, saying a review of 200 registrations found nearly 40% appeared to be US-born.

The Justice Department declined to confirm or deny its use of subpoenas in noncitizen voter investigations, but said it “will enforce the law wherever the evidence leads.” The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to questions.

Some election officials and lawyers told Reuters the noncitizen voting investigations could bolster a false narrative that American elections are vulnerable to widespread fraud. In a closely divided country, Trump and his allies could use those claims to attack the legitimacy of narrow defeats, particularly in tightly contested races, they said.

The subpoenas issued by the administration are “clearly a distraction” for local and state election officials, said Paul Charlton, a former US attorney for Arizona in the Republican administration of George W. Bush. “In my time as a federal prosecutor, we prosecuted people who shouldn’t have voted, but it was so infrequent as to never even come close to altering the outcome of an election.”

Since Trump returned to office, prosecutors have accused at least 147 people of illegally voting under a federal “voting by aliens” statute, including 102 since the start of September, according to a Reuters analysis of court filings and federal records. The cases – most of which remain unresolved – amount to fewer than one for every million people who voted in 2024.

The investigations are “setting up” post-election challenges that, while legally weak, could sow chaos, said Ben Berwick, a former Justice Department attorney who served in the Obama and Trump administrations and now leads the election law and litigation team at Protect Democracy, an advocacy group. Trump-aligned candidates who lose could argue that suspected noncitizen votes made it impossible to determine the rightful winner and seek to have ballots or even the election result thrown out, Berwick said.

The stakes are high. Democrats need to gain four Senate seats and five House seats to take control of Congress. Winning either chamber would give them power to launch investigations into the Trump administration and Trump family business dealings.

A BROADENING SEARCH

The subpoenas identified by Reuters varied widely in scope, from records on individual voters to demands for entire local voter rolls containing tens of thousands of names. None of the jurisdictions contacted said they were resisting the subpoenas.

In the US, subpoenas are legally binding orders requiring recipients to testify or produce documents or other evidence.

In Minnesota, a traditionally Democratic state with an unexpectedly competitive US Senate race, the Trump administration issued subpoenas for voting records on dozens of people in the Minneapolis-area counties of Anoka and Hennepin, where the administration has carried out a major federal immigration crackdown. To date, the Justice Department has charged at least eight people from the two counties with voting as noncitizens. All the cases are ongoing and no one has been convicted.

In California, the Justice Department has issued at least 17 subpoenas to governments in Democratic-leaning jurisdictions, including Los Angeles and San Diego counties. The state is home to at least two districts with competitive US House races and is typically slow to count ballots, with final results sometimes taking weeks.

Some voting experts said the Trump administration and its allies could use the period before California finishes counting ballots to amplify allegations of noncitizen voting and challenge the legitimacy of close races. Reuters also identified previously unreported subpoenas seeking voter records that were issued to Marin County and Fresno County. Fresno lies within California's 22nd Congressional District, a closely watched midterm battleground.

In Philadelphia, a Democratic stronghold, local officials confirmed receiving at least four subpoenas for voting records. In reliably Democratic Massachusetts, one of the states where federal courts blocked the administration’s voter roll demands, a Trump-backed US attorney has targeted at least eight cities and towns with grand jury subpoenas, six of them not previously reported, Reuters found.

At least three of the Massachusetts subpoenas required officials to provide alist of all registered voters,including names, addresses, party affiliations, birth dates, voting status and voter identification numbers. An accompanying letter, obtained from one city through a public records request, urged recipients “not to disclose the existence of this subpoena or the fact of your compliance therewith, to anyone,” but said the request for secrecy was not mandatory.

In Lynn, Massachusetts, a city with a large Hispanic population, federal prosecutors subpoenaed records for 25 to 30 people. “Up until now, they’ve found one instance of someone voting in an election that shouldn’t have been voting,” James Lamanna, the city’s clerk and election chief, told Reuters. “This doesn’t reach the level of something serious and pervasive that it would jeopardize the integrity of an election.”

Other states where subpoenas have been issued include Arizona, Washington, New York, Connecticut, Utah and Michigan.

CLAIMS UNDER SCRUTINY

Trump has repeatedly portrayed noncitizen voting as a grave threat to election integrity. The Heritage Foundation, a conservative think tank that has raised similar concerns for years, argues that weak verification procedures create opportunities for illegal voting and that voter fraud could affect the outcome of a close election.

Voting-rights groups counter that repeated reviews have found no evidence of noncitizen voting on a scale that has changed an election outcome. Thousands of noncitizens have been mistakenly registered to vote because of clerical errors or software glitches, often while obtaining driver’s licenses, but state and local officials say only a small fraction actually cast ballots.

In a nationally televised address in July, Trump said his administration had identified more than 275,000 noncitizen voters, which the White House said were in four Democratic-leaning states. State officials disputed those assertions. In Nevada, federal officials initially claimed to have identified nearly 16,000 potential noncitizens on the voter rolls before revising the figure to fewer than 200. Nevada officials later concluded those remaining individuals were all citizens.

Federal prosecutors are continuing to report suspected new cases. In Washington state this week, they said they had identified more than 400 noncitizens who appear to be registered to vote. They asked state election officials to set aside any current ballots from those individuals until their citizenship could be verified. The Washington secretary of state's office told Reuters it has received about 60 federal subpoenas in recent weeks seeking information on individual voters.

The administration has also intensified its enforcement efforts. On October 19, the Justice Department said it had charged 28 people in California, all legal permanent residents, with voting as noncitizens or making false statements on voting or naturalization paperwork. California election officials have called the campaign a politically motivated distraction, noting that the cases uncovered so far amount to a tiny fraction of the state’s more than 23 million registered voters.

The administration has also threatened legal consequences for election officials who resist its demands. California officials objected after federal authorities threatened to prosecute election officials who did not act on the list of 20,000 alleged noncitizen voters. Acting US Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, who spearheaded the administration’s claims in California, acknowledged last week that the list could include US citizens.

“We’re not perfect,” he said.

items.title: AI-related investment, consumers likely boosted US economic growth in third quarter
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 29 (Reuters) - US economic growth likely accelerated in the third quarter as resilient consumer spending and AI-driven business investment more than offset the impact of higher oil prices stemming from the conflict in the Middle East.

The anticipated strength would stand in stark contrast to households' downbeat assessment of the economy, reflected in President Donald Trump's record-low approval ratings and a sharp deterioration in consumer sentiment. The Commerce Department will publish its advance estimate of third-quarter gross domestic product on Thursday, less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will determine control of Congress.

"People are very upset about high energy and food prices, and yet the fundamentals for consumers are still decent," said Gus Faucher, chief economist at PNC Financial. "We still have job growth, wage gains and there's the strong stock market that's supporting spending by high-income households, in particular, so consumers continue to increase their spending at a pretty steady clip."

GDP likely increased at a 3.2% annualized rate last quarter, a Reuters survey of economists predicted. The economy grew at a 2.2% pace in the April-June quarter. But the survey was conducted before the release on Wednesday of September's advance economic indicators report, which showed a widening of the goods trade deficit as strong demand for capital goods linked to the AI spending boom lifted imports to a record high.

Economists estimated the trade shortfall subtracted at least 4 percentage points from GDP growth last quarter. But the drag was probably blunted by the AI-related investment, with business spending on equipment expected to have notched a third straight quarter of double-digit growth.

AI also likely contributed to spending on intellectual property products. Inventories are also expected to have added to GDP growth last quarter.

Investors are increasingly focusing on the rising costs of long-term AI projects in which the payoff is uncertain. Tech firms have borrowed huge sums over the past year for AI spending, a potential downside risk to equipment spending. Still, economists did not expect this to hinder the economy.

"There's likely to be more discretion when it comes to investment in AI, but the underlying momentum remains quite strong," said Gregory Daco, chief economist at EY-Parthenon. "AI-related investment is likely to remain a key pillar of US economic activity, even if there are some risks of pullbacks and some questions as to the return on all of its investment."

The economy is expanding at a pace that is well above what some Federal Reserve officials regard as the non-inflationary growth rate of around 2%. The US central bank on Wednesday left its benchmark interest rate in the 3.75%-4.00% range while acknowledging that inflation "remains elevated."

Economists expected the Fed to raise rates in December. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh told reporters that "economic activity is expanding at a strong pace," noting that "while uncertainty remains, owing in part to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient."

ROBUST CONSUMER SPENDING EXPECTED

Consumer spending, which accounts for more than two-thirds of the economy, is projected to have increased at above a 3.0% pace after growing at a 3.8% rate in the second quarter. Historic low layoffs and moderate hiring are helping to underpin spending, though wage gains have at times lagged inflation.

Households have been saving less and dipping into their nest eggs to fund spending. With average gasoline prices still above $4 a gallon as the US-Israeli war with Iran drags on, economists anticipated that consumer spending would pull back.

"It appears that households made a judgment when the conflict began earlier this year that the run-up in energy prices would prove mostly temporary," said Stephen Stanley, chief US economist at Santander US Capital Markets. "That assessment may prove wrong, so consumers may need, at some point, to tighten their belts."

Rising mortgage rates because of the Middle East conflict are expected to have pushed residential investment back into contraction last quarter. Higher borrowing costs have overshadowed a moderation in house prices, putting homeownership out of the reach of young adults.

Homebuilding is also being constrained by land and labor shortages amid an immigration crackdown, and higher prices for materials due to tariffs on imports. The construction of data centers to support AI likely lifted business investment in nonresidential structures after stabilizing in the second quarter. A rebound in government spending is anticipated.

A measure of domestic demand, which excludes inventories, trade and government, is expected to have surged last quarter. Final sales to private domestic purchasers grew at a 4.6% rate in the second quarter.

"The overall picture is that the economy is growing at a decent pace, but the primary factors are an AI-driven investment boom and consumption driven primarily by rising stock wealth," said Dean Baker, senior economist at the Center for Economic and Policy Research. "It's unclear how long this can continue, but this is not a very stable picture, nor a very positive one for most working people."

items.title: Cyberattack concealed political spending by big donors before US midterm elections
items.content_html:
NEW YORK, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The Federal Election Commission restored its electronic filing system Wednesday night after taking it offline for nearly 41 hours to contain a cyberattack, which temporarily concealed spending from big donors as political donations ramp up in the final days of the midterms.

Campaign watchdogs sounded alarms as the outage dragged into its third evening. Super PACs and other groups could not file mandatory 24- and 48-hour reports that show how much money they are spending to help or hurt candidates at the polls, shrouding the most recent political spending from public view.

"We didn't have access to the last-minute spending, which is really ramped up as the election draws nearer," said campaign finance watchdog Molly White, who tracks crypto and Big Tech political spending. "We have no visibility into that when the filing systems are down."

"It's pretty devastating this close to the election," she added.

The outage came at a critical time as daily spending accelerates to its fastest pace in the two-year election cycle, campaign finance experts said. Super PACs, which can accept and give unlimited amounts of money, and dark money groups spent an average of over $50 million per day the week before the outage, OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin said. More than $250 million in spending was reported on October 20 alone, he added.

The FEC told users that most of the services affected by the outage have been restored. It posted a notice just after 10 p.m. ET on Monday saying it was investigating a problem that caused "major" outages across its systems that process electronic campaign filings.

Reuters could not establish the motive for the hacking effort. Hackers of all stripes regularly target government networks for espionage, financial gain or political motives.

The FEC does not play a role in administering US elections and the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots.

“Disclosure delayed is disclosure denied,” Hilary Braseth, executive director of nonpartisan campaign finance watchdog OpenSecrets, said in a statement released before the system was restored. “When hundreds of millions of dollars in outside money flood political airwaves in the final days before an election, transparency is not an optional luxury, it is a fundamental public safeguard.”

The FEC did not return requests for comment Wednesday and did not announce any details on the cause of the outage. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency and the FBI both referred questions to the FEC.

An FEC officer told campaign compliance firms late Monday that it took those services offline after a "bad actor" tried to breach the agency's systems, according to an email reviewed by Reuters.

Campaign finance managers had to reset their passwords before logging in to the system, according to an email reviewed by Reuters.

The timing of the hacking attempt this close to the November 3 elections, and lack of information from the FEC, stirred up conspiracy theories throughout the industry, several people said. White noted that it would be a good way for unscrupulous actors to hide unpopular last-minute spending.

"It's hard to say with any real information that that's what happened, but it's certainly I think where people's minds go very quickly," she said.

Kyle Sandy, the cybersecurity director at IT security firm Logically, said taking the system offline is the right call when dealing with an attack.

"It tells me the FEC detected something they couldn't immediately scope and chose a known outage over an unknown risk," Sandy said, giving the agency time to ensure none of its data was altered by the hackers before bringing it back online.

items.title: Warsh says politics played no role in Fed's rate decision by group he is 'honored' to lead
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh on Wednesday said he is "honored" to lead the central bank's policymakers and said politics played no role in their decision to skip a rate hike, rebutting at least indirectly President Donald Trump's allegation that the Fed Board is partisan and against him.

“We just came out of a heck of a family fight” at the latest Federal Open Market Committee meeting, Warsh told reporters after the Fed ended a two-day meeting with a decision to leave the policy rate in the 3.75%-4.00%range.

“I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment, and I'm honored to be here and honored to be the chairman of this group,” he said.

“Politics played no role in the decision," Warsh added. "I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs. I didn't hear an utterance about politics. I didn't hear a reference to politics, elections, what's happening in the next week."

Elections to be held on November 3 will determine if Trump's Republican Party retains its majorities in the House and Senate. Voters say affordability concerns, exemplified both by ongoing inflation as well as high borrowing costs, are top of mind as they head to the polls.

Warsh said he and his colleagues will get plenty of data in coming weeks that will leave them "better positioned" in December to determine whether to raise rates, and though the coming period will be "information-rich," it will have "nothing to do" with politics.

Trump, during both his first and second terms in the White House, has excoriated the central bank for failing to deliver big rate cuts, and after the Fed's decision in September to raise rates blamed Warsh's colleagues as "hostile" and "partisan."

Trump has not attacked Warsh himself, as he routinely did the previous Fed Chair Jerome Powell, and on Wednesday Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said both he and the president have "great confidence that Chair Warsh will steer the Fed between the right combination of growth and inflation."

On Wednesday, Trump told reporters he had not spoken with Warsh about the central bank's decision.

Still, Wednesday's news conference demonstrated the minefield Warsh is traversing to remain in Trump's good graces while also trying to assure financial markets that he will credibly fight still-elevated inflation.

The administration continues to press the case against rate hikes, and Bessent told CNBC on Wednesday that while "some" on the Fed Board feel letting inflation stay so high for so long shows "a lack of will, I don't think it has to."

Fed Governor Lisa Cook was one of two dissenters on Wednesday's decision, preferring another quarter-point interest-rate hike instead of the hold that the Fed's 10 other rate-setters agreed to.

Trump has been trying to fire Cook for more than a year, with a possible White House administrative proceeding set for November 5, and has also called for Powell to vacate his seat on the central bank's Board of Governors. The two matters have high stakes for the Fed's status as an independent policy-making body.

Asked if he would be involved in the White House proceedings against Cook, however, Warsh said, "not to my knowledge."

Warsh was chosen by Trump to succeed Powell, who was also appointed by Trump to lead the Fed. Powell quickly fell afoul of the president for not following his advice on monetary policy.

As Warsh took over the Fed in late May, Trump said he was confident Warsh would lower rates and that he would not have selected him for the job if he did not feel that was the case.

Instead, persistent inflation and market doubts about Warsh's independence led the new Fed chief to take a hardline position in pledging to defend the Fed's 2% inflation target, with a rate hike in September and more considered likely.

So far, Trump has given Warsh the benefit of the doubt, blaming the rate rise on a group of governors appointed by former President Joe Biden that includes Cook.

items.title: Dolores Huerta, US labor leader and force for human rights, dies at 96
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - Dolores Huerta, who co-founded the United Farm Workers (UFW) with Cesar Chavez and fought legislators and powerful growers in the US to improve the lives of a previously powerless constituency, died on Wednesday at the age of 96, her family said in a statement.

Huerta was one of the foremost women in US labor history, serving the UFW as chief negotiator, strike organizer, lobbyist and reformer during its heyday in the 1960s and '70s in California's agriculture-rich Central Valley.

Thanks to the contracts the UFW negotiated, farmworkers won job security, healthcare, retirement plans, a credit union and job-specific benefits such as guaranteed rest periods, toilets in the fields, clean drinking water and protection from pesticides.

Huerta was credited with giving the UFW its slogan "Si, se puede," the loose translation of which, "Yes, we can," was later used by Barack Obama during his successful 2008 presidential campaign.

She remained a regular on the college lecture circuit into her 90s, speaking out against the immigration policies of President Donald Trump. During elections she traveled the country, endorsing candidates and registering voters.

UFW co-founder Chavez, who died in 1993 and was the face of the organization, was a seventh-grade dropout and former grape picker with a man-of-the-soil appeal who espoused the non-violent philosophies of Gandhi and Martin Luther King, with a nod to Emiliano Zapata, a leader of Mexico's peasant revolution in the early 20th century.

But Chavez had a dark side. In 2026, Huerta was one of a number of women who came forward with accounts of how they had been sexually assaulted by him, in some cases when they were minors. Huerta said that he had pressured her into having sex one time, and another time raped her. Both encounters resulted in pregnancies, and Huerta said she arranged for the babies to be raised by others.

OUT OF THE SPOTLIGHT

While Chavez was recruiting, going on well-publicized hunger strikes and being embraced by liberal lawmakers and celebrities, the diminutive, college-educated Huerta handled negotiating with growers, lobbying legislators and other business for the UFW.

She was arrested more than 20 times, subjected to death threats and other harassment. She suffered broken ribs and a damaged spleen when beaten by baton-wielding San Francisco police in a 1988 protest against the policies of George H.W. Bush during his presidential campaign.

In an interview with PBS in 2012, before the assault accusations against Chavez came to light, Huerta said she had been fine with him taking the spotlight as she wanted to focus on helping people rather than gaining fame.

"He said, 'One of us is going to have to be the spokesperson. Are you all right if I'm the spokesperson?' Of course, I said yes."

STANDING UP

Huerta was born in Dawson, New Mexico, to a Mexican immigrant family, and spent much of her youth in Stockton, California, after her parents divorced. Her father was a miner, laborer, union activist and state lawmaker; her mother raised three children while buying and running a hotel for low-income people in Stockton.

Huerta's mother instilled a spirit of activism in her daughter. Huerta was into her second marriage when she became a schoolteacher, but that career did not last long.

"I couldn't stand seeing kids come to class hungry and needing shoes," she said. "I thought I could do more by organizing farmworkers than by trying to teach their hungry children."

She registered voters in Stockton and founded the Agricultural Workers Association before meeting Chavez and joining him in starting the National Farm Workers Association in 1962. In 1965 they began a series of strikes and boycotts that would last five years against various California grape growers and eventually spread to lettuce growers.

During that period the organization evolved into the United Farm Workers and picked up support from King and New York Senator Robert F. Kennedy. Not eating a grape — unless it had a union label — became a political statement in the United States.

The boycotts and strikes sometimes became contentious. In addition to industry opposition, the UFW found itself up against California Governor Ronald Reagan, who denounced the UFW as immoral and made a point of eating grapes on television.

COLLECTIVE BARGAINING

One by one, growers began signing contracts with the UFW and in 1975 Huerta's work also helped bring about another victory — passage of the California Agricultural Labor Relations Act, the first law in the US that gave farmworkers collective bargaining rights.

Huerta said that being a woman gave her an edge at the negotiating table with growers.

"They really didn't know how to respond because they couldn't do the usual forceful type of thing," she told PBS. "And when you would bring up to them and show them the conditions that the workers were working under, and they were kind of embarrassed, actually."

In 2012, Obama presented Huerta with the Presidential Medal of Freedom, the country's highest civilian award.

Her life was the basis of the award-winning film "Dolores" that was shown at the Sundance Film Festival in 2017.

While the UFW's influence abated, Huerta's activism did not. In 2002 she established the Dolores Huerta Foundation for community activism with her daughter Camila Chavez as its executive director. She pushed for changes in immigration laws, voter registration, women's rights and Obama's healthcare reform.

Huerta, who said she remained close to the two children she had with Chavez, also had two children from her first marriage, five from her second and four from a long-term relationship with Richard Chavez, brother of Cesar and another key UFW figure, who died in 2011.

items.title: One injured in fire at South Carolina nuclear site; no contamination reported
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - A fire on Wednesday at a South Carolina complex that produced plutonium and tritium for nuclear weapons during the Cold War left one person with minor injuries, a US Department of Energy spokesperson said.

The spokesperson, citing officials at the Savannah River Site that includes the Savannah River National Laboratory where the fire was reported, said the fire was extinguished and no contamination has been reported. The spokesperson said the person injured was an employee who was taken to the hospital.

The Savannah River Site did not say what caused the fire.

The fire prompted a "site area emergency." The Federal Aviation Administration temporarily restricted flights in the area because of the fire, according to its website. The Savannah River Site said rail, river and ground travel in the area also was restricted and that employees not involved in emergency response or shutdown operations were sheltered as a precaution.

After producing material for nuclear weapons during the Cold War, the Savannah River National Laboratory now focuses on waste cleanup and nuclear materials management.

It was built near Jackson, South Carolina, in the early 1950s.

items.title: EXCLUSIVE: US, Canada working on deal to ease steel, auto tariffs, sources say
items.content_html:
OTTAWA/WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - The United States and Canada are working on a deal to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, two US and four Canadian sources said, as the two governments try to repair relations that soured after trade talks broke down in August.

The talks focus on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to 50% tariff on Canadian steel and a 25% tariff on autos, with negotiators discussing potential relief from those duties.

Just 32% of Americans approve of US President Donald Trump and his Republican Party risks losing control of Congress in next week's midterm elections. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a political liability for Trump, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada.

One Canadian source briefed on the negotiations said a deal on steel and auto tariffs was possible before the November 3 elections, while US sources said the Trump administration wanted Canada to make further concessions. The sources spoke on condition of anonymity because the talks are private.

The Section 232 tariffs are administered by the Commerce Department, putting Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick rather than the US Trade Representative's office at the center of the negotiations, sources on both sides of the border said.

Lutnick and Canada's Dominic LeBlanc, the minister responsible for Canada-US trade, have been in regular contact recently, one of the sources said.

"Canada remains in constructive dialogue with our U.S. counterparts on a range of priorities," a spokesperson for LeBlanc, said in a statement. "We stand ready to work constructively and in good faith towards a more mutually beneficial trading relationship that respects Canada’s interests.”

The US Trade Representative's Office and Canada have also been in contact in recent days regarding the overall architecture of any deal and all other trade issues, a USTR official said.

The White House and the Commerce Department did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

OTTAWA SEES PROGRESS

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks with the United States, adding that Ottawa had not changed its stance.

"To the extent any progress has been made, it's because the US is coming closer to our position," he told reporters, but did not give details.

A Canadian industry source said a deal could come quickly, but not necessarily a broad one. "If it happens, it'll happen fast. But my sense is it'll be a narrowed deal, if it even happens,” the source said.

Another Canadian source said they have believed for some time that a deal on Section 232 tariffs is likely before the midterms. Any agreement would be driven by Trump and Carney, the source said, adding that both leaders had said a mutually beneficial deal is possible.

Carney has said he wants a good deal for Canada.

US and Canadian trade talks collapsed in August over issues such as whether to cut duties on medium- and heavy-duty vehicles that are critical for Canadian factories. US automakers had hoped the trade talks would deliver relief from Washington's original 25% tariffs that have raised the cost of shipping vehicles and parts across the border.

Trump has previously announced that he would raise the tariffs on steel and auto imports from Canada to 50% from January 1, 2027. At a political rally on Sunday, Trump predicted the trade dispute would be resolved "soon," without providing specifics.

Trump signed an order on Friday to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit businesses in Maine.

items.title: Screwworm infests dog in Arizona, widening US cases
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - New World screwworm, a parasitic fly that eats warm-blooded animals alive, has infested a dog in Arizona, widening cases to a third US state, the US Department of Agriculture said on Wednesday.

The first detection in Arizona was in Cochise County, which borders Mexico, according to the USDA.

The dog had a wound on its back that was infested with maggots, consistent with screwworm, and scientific testing verified the infestation, the Arizona Department of Agriculture said. The dog was receiving veterinary care, it added.

"We have been preparing for this possibility for a long while and are acting swiftly," State Veterinarian Dr. Ryan Wolker said in a statement.

The Arizona case marks the latest sign that screwworm, eradicated from the US decades ago, may be regaining a foothold despite federal efforts to contain it, complicating the USDA's attempts to reopen livestock trade with Mexico and ease record beef prices ahead of the midterm elections.

The USDA said it was restricting animal movement in a 20-km (12-mile) zone around the case, increasing surveillance of live animals and releasing sterile flies that combat screwworm in response to the infestation.

The agency halted livestock imports from Mexico last year to try to keep out screwworm, which advanced north through Mexico and Latin America. It detected screwworm in a calf in Texas in June and then confirmed additional cases in Texas and New Mexico.

As of Wednesday, the agency had reported 71 screwworm cases since June, and 18 were active, according to its website. Infestations have multiplied since last month, when there were only two active cases.

The import halt helped tighten US cattle supplies and push beef prices to record highs for American consumers, raising concerns about affordability ahead of the midterm elections.

The USDA began to resume livestock imports from Mexico in August and has restarted trade at three ports of entry in Arizona and New Mexico. The agency has said it next plans to resume imports from Mexico in Nogales, Arizona, on November 30, if conditions for safe trade are in place.

Last week, the USDA confirmed the first case of screwworm in US wildlife in an elk in Texas.

items.title: Last Republican incumbent senator in a Democratic-leaning state fights for survival
items.content_html:
WINDHAM, Maine, Oct 27 (Reuters) - If Republican Senator Susan Collins wins this nail-biter of an election, it may well be because voters in Maine decide she is not Republican enough.

Since her first victory in 1996, Collins’ reputation as an independent-minded moderate has helped her win reelection even as Maine backed Democrats for president. Now the only Republican incumbent running in a Democratic-leaning state, she is deadlocked in opinion polls with Democrat Troy Jackson in a race that could help determine control of the US Senate.

Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of the 100-seat Senate from Republicans in the November 3 midterm elections. Jackson, a rough-hewn former logger and state Senate president, has attacked Collins as a rubber stamp for Republican President Donald Trump.

Collins is countering with the clout she has amassed over her 30-year Senate career, highlighting projects she has funded and carve-outs she has secured to lessen the economic fallout from Trump’s spending cuts, tariffs and war with Iran.

“If it wasn't Susan Collins, this race would have been over three months ago,” said Maine Democratic consultant Toby McGrath.

But strategists in both parties say the pool of the independent-minded, persuadable voters who backed Collins in previous elections has shrunk as partisan lines have hardened and Trump has galvanized Democrats in opposition.

“If you hate Trump, you're voting for whoever the Democrats put on the ballot,” said Phil Harriman, a former Republican state senator.

Democrats faced a potential debacle this summer, when Graham Platner, an oyster farmer and Marine veteran, won the party’s nomination only to drop out after facing a rape accusation that he denied.

The party quickly united behind Jackson, who has invoked his hardscrabble upbringing in the remote logging town of Allagash as he campaigns on a populist agenda of universal healthcare and raising taxes on the wealthy.

“I saw at a young age how people with money and power and influence can hold people back,” he said at a campaign event on Saturday.

$1.5 BILLION IN EARMARKS

In recent weeks, Collins has visited projects she has funded through her work on the powerful Senate Appropriations Committee: a wastewater treatment plant in North Windham, a dock in Bucksport, an emergency center in Farmington. She says she has secured nearly $1.5 billion in earmarks since 2021.

“This has required hard work, knowledge and seniority. The question for voters in this campaign is who can do more for Maine,” she said at an October 15 debate.

That influence, she argues, has also helped to shield Maine from the Trump administration’s policies.

As Trump’s trade war with Canada has hammered the state’s economy, Collins has pointed to tariff exemptions the administration has granted at her request for road salt, cement and equipment used by the state’s blueberry, potato and apple growers.

The Trump administration also credited her when it released home-heating oil reserves to try to drive down prices that have increased more than 70% since last year – a crucial issue in a state where roughly half of households rely on the product.

Collins has also pointed to a $50 billion fund she crafted to help rural hospitals cope with healthcare cuts in the 2025 tax and spending package that enacted most of Trump’s legislative agenda, as well as money for body-worn cameras and de-escalation training for federal immigration agents following the January killing of two US citizens in Minnesota.

'THERE SHOULDN'T BE A LIST'

Jackson argues that these carve-outs amount to little when weighed against the damage caused by Trump.

Body cameras and de-escalation training did not stop an immigration agent from killing a state resident in July, he says, and residents would not be struggling to heat their homes if Trump had not started the war with Iran, which has pushed up oil prices globally.

Trump’s trade war with Canada, he argues, is only possible because Republicans in Congress have surrendered their authority over tariffs to Trump.

“I can't believe that the most powerful US senator in the world would stand there and say, 'Well, I got this and this and that off the list,' instead of the fact that there shouldn’t be a list,” he said on Saturday.

SIX ADS IN A ROW

Meanwhile, a relentless ad war has played out over the state’s airwaves. AdImpact, an analysis firm, estimates $199 million will be spent on the race – equal to $170 for every adult in the state.

During a local newscast on Friday, six ads in a row were devoted to the contest.

Those ads are chasing a small slice of undecided voters.

Democratic activists say they are encountering relatively few people who have yet to decide on a candidate as they campaign door-to-door in Windham, a Portland suburb that backed Collins by a 14-point margin in 2020, even as it backed Democrat Joe Biden over Trump for president.

“There’s just a lot less of that persuadable middle than we historically see,” said volunteer Austin Coco.

Windham resident Jim Tabor, a retired optician, said he has grown disillusioned with the Republican Party under Trump. A Collins supporter in past elections, he said this year he will back Jackson.

“If he turns out to be a bum, I’ll vote against him next time. But Susan Collins won’t be there,” he said.

items.title: Norway joins the list of countries Trump has abused in vulgar terms
items.content_html:
PORT HURON, Michigan, Oct 25 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump on Sunday escalated his invective against Norway, calling it a "shit house country" and saying Norwegian immigrants were not welcome in the United States because the Nobel committee, based in the capital Oslo, had not awarded him a Peace Prize.

  • Trump made the comments at a political rally in Port Huron, Michigan, ahead of next week's midterm elections
  • Attributing recent unrest in France to immigration, Trump said he would welcome immigrants from some countries but not from Norway "because I didn't get the Nobel Prize ... So I don't want anybody from Norway"
  • There was no indication that the Trump administration was adopting new official policy on Norwegian immigrants
  • "He knows very well that the Nobel Committee is independent. We have reminded them of that, if anyone is wondering, and that is still the case," Norwegian Foreign Minister Espen Barth Eide told national broadcaster NRK on Monday. His ministry declined to comment further
  • "Norway has become a shit house country, actually," Trump said, using a term that he has previously applied to Haiti, Libya, Somalia and Yemen
  • Norway is among the highest-income countries as measured by GDP per capita, according to International Monetary Fund data, opens new tab. Norway's sovereign wealth fund posted a record profit of 1.75 trillion Norwegian crowns ($184.3 billion) for the first half of 2026
  • The Norwegian Nobel Committee did not immediately return requests for comment
  • Trump earlier this month called the failure to give him a Nobel Peace Prize an "indelible stain" on Norway

items.title: Biden-era officials who quit over Gaza urge 2028 candidates to denounce policy architects
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - US officials who had resigned from former President Joe Biden's administration over his Gaza policy said on Wednesday that Democratic presidential candidates for the 2028 race should denounce that policy and its architects.

  • Twelve former US officials who quit the Biden administration between late 2023 and mid-2024 over US support for Israeli attacks on Gaza signed a joint statement, opens new tab
  • "We call on candidates for the 2028 Presidential Nomination to commit to not hire any administration official directly responsible for enabling Israel's military actions in Gaza," they said in the statement released on Wednesday.
  • A video released with the statement showed images of Biden-era officials like former Secretary of State Antony Blinken and former national security adviser Jake Sullivan, among others.
  • The Democratic Biden administration had faced protests from some progressive lawmakers and activists over the Gaza policy.
  • Progressive Democrats like US Representative Rashida Tlaib and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani have opposed US support for Israel over Israeli attacks in Gaza and Lebanon, the US-Israeli war on Iran and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's close ties to Republicans, leading to an erosion of Democratic backing for Washington's ally.
  • The 12 former officials said the 2028 presidential candidates should "acknowledge the complicity of the United States government in Israel's genocide in Gaza."
  • Multiple rights groups, experts, scholars and UN inquiries have assessed that Israel's devastating assault on Gaza amounts to genocide.
  • Israel has called its actions self-defense after a deadly attack by Hamas-led militants on Israel in October 2023.
