  • Blinken and Sullivan have expressed concerns about civilian killings in Gaza even as the Biden administration maintained diplomatic and military support for Israel.

items.title: Michigan Senate race a test of attacks on Muslim candidate, progressive agenda
items.content_html:
Oct 28 (Reuters) - Michigan's tight race for an open US Senate seat will help determine control of the chamber while testing two broader questions: whether identity-based attacks on a Muslim candidate can succeed in a battleground state, and how willing Democratic voters are to embrace the party's progressive wing.

Republican Mike Rogers has sought to portray Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who would be the nation's first Muslim senator if he wins the November 3 election, as sympathetic to Islamist extremism, which El-Sayed denies and supporters say is Islamophobic. Rogers has also argued that El-Sayed's support for universal healthcare and other progressive policies places him outside the political mainstream.

El-Sayed, a former public health official, has focused his campaign on lowering costs for working-class Americans while seeking to tie Rogers to President Donald Trump, even as Rogers has broken with the president on some issues in the campaign's closing weeks.

Trump has falsely accused El-Sayed of being a Muslim extremist, while Rogers has tried to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood. Branches of the Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist movements, were designated as terrorist organizations by the Trump administration this year.

El-Sayed has disavowed the group and denied any connection with it. Pollsters and political strategists say the attacks are aimed at dissuading Jewish and Black voters in the Detroit area who backed his primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, from voting for him.

"He's a Muslim-American and so Rogers is attempting to do his best to portray El-Sayed as an outsider who's dangerous," said Jonathan Hanson, a political scientist and public policy lecturer at the University of Michigan.

Michigan's Senate seat is critical to both parties' efforts to control the chamber. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority heading into Tuesday's election.

Independent analysts rate the race a toss-up. The RealClearPolling average shows El-Sayed ahead by 2.5 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 1.4 points in 2024.

El-Sayed campaign spokesperson Cole Wozniak accused Rogers of resorting to "desperate, bad faith attacks" and said the Democrat was focused on "his plans to bring down costs and stand up to the chaos and corruption in Washington."

Abby Ronson, a spokesperson for the Rogers campaign, pointed to Rogers' appearance on Sunday on NBC News' "Meet the Press," where he said he was not criticizing Islam but what he described as El-Sayed's adherence to a "radical Islamic agenda."

IDENTITY ATTACKS

Advocating policies to curb corporate influence and expand the social safety net, El-Sayed, 41, has emerged as one of the Democratic Party's most prominent progressives. He describes himself as a capitalist and rejects the socialist label, but a victory on Tuesday would likely be seen as a boost for the party's left wing as it seeks greater influence ahead of the 2028 presidential election.

But the margin of any victory will matter, said Michigan State University political scientist Matt Grossmann.

"If El-Sayed wins by a couple of points but trails Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson by a wide margin, that won't be a very convincing argument," Grossmann said. "And if El-Sayed were to lose, then it would be a mark against that faction of the party."

Rogers, 63, has cast himself as a pragmatic conservative focused on lowering costs, boosting manufacturing and strengthening border security. With Trump's popularity sagging, he recently called for an end to the war in Iran and the trade dispute with Canada, while avoiding direct criticism of the president.

But portraying El-Sayed as a national security threat has also become a central feature of Rogers' closing message. Rogers has based that claim in part on a 2012 group letter signed by El-Sayed and other Egyptian Americans in support of then-newly elected Egyptian President Mohamed Morsi, who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood. The letter called on Morsi to purge the media and security services of holdovers from the dictatorship toppled during the Arab Spring.

The El-Sayed campaign did not immediately respond to a query about the letter.

Earlier this month Rogers agreed with a social media post calling El-Sayed a terrorist. He also appeared with Trump at a rally on Sunday where the president likened El-Sayed to the September 11 attackers and said his goal was to keep a "jihadist" out of the Senate.

The rhetoric prompted a rare rebuke from the NAACP, the nonpartisan civil rights organization, which does not typically intervene in political races.

"The blatantly racist attacks surrounding the Michigan Senate race are unacceptable and disgusting," NAACP President Derrick Johnson said in a statement. "It’s the same ugly, divisive tactics we’ve seen used during the darkest chapters of the South’s history."

A poll by Michigan State University's Institute for Public Policy and Social Research found that 38% of Michigan voters were less likely to support a Muslim candidate.

John Clark, a political science professor at Western Michigan University, said the attacks on El-Sayed were aimed in part at depressing Democratic turnout but could work against Rogers by angering and boosting turnout among Michigan's sizable Arab American communities in Dearborn and elsewhere.

"Maybe this helps with some voters, but it has the potential of backfiring with others," Clark said.

items.title: Eleven shot near Florida A&M university in Tallahassee
items.content_html:
Oct 25 (Reuters) - A shooting near a Florida university campus in Tallahassee on Saturday night left 11 people with gunshot wounds and another injured, authorities said.

The shooting took place near Florida Agricultural & Mechanical University's campus on Perry Street, the university said, while police counted six adults and six juveniles among the injured.

"At least three of the shooting victims have sustained serious injuries, while nine others are reported to be in stable condition," the Tallahassee police said in a statement.

Initial findings showed a "physical altercation" preceded the shooting, police said, without elaborating.

"It is especially heartbreaking to know that children are among those injured," said police chief Lawrence Revell.

The youngest of those shot was 11, the NY Post newspaper said, but police did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment.

An altercation at a homecoming party escalated into gunfire and a fight between two or three individuals led to shots being fired just before 8 p.m., the paper added.

Police said their violent crimes unit was investigating the circumstances.

"The safety and security of our students, faculty, and staff remain our highest priority," Florida A&M said on X.

items.title: Inside the Trump-administration campaign to return Brazil’s Bolsonaro clan to power
items.content_html:
SAO PAULO, Oct 24 (Reuters) - Two US State Department officials led a campaign to restore the right-wing Bolsonaro clan to power in Brazil and successfully pushed for sanctions aimed at tilting the election in their favor, according to 10 current and former US officials with direct knowledge of the matter.

Their plan faces a reckoning on Sunday, when Senator Flavio Bolsonaro faces leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva in a tight run-off. Lula has warned Washington against encroaching on Brazil's sovereignty and accused his opponent of plotting with the Trump administration.

The two officials were Darren Beattie, a Senior Advisor for Western Hemisphere Affairs who oversees Brazil policy, and Ricardo Pita, another senior advisor promoted this year to Deputy Assistant Secretary for North America. The details of their campaign to return the Bolsonaros to power haven't been previously reported.

Beattie and Pita, both political appointees, operated with wide latitude to manage Washington's relationship with the second most-populous country in the Americas, the people said.

In the months before election campaigning began, they instructed US diplomats in Brazil that it was US policy to restore former President Jair Bolsonaro as Brazil’s leader – even though he had been disqualified from office for plotting a coup in 2022, when he lost the presidential election to Lula, three of the people said.

After Bolsonaro received a 27-year sentence in September 2025, the two men pivoted to supporting the candidacy of his son, right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, the three sources said. Beattie and Pita told embassy staff not to interact with other conservative presidential contenders who could challenge the younger Bolsonaro, they said.

Since last year, the two men have successfully advocated for punitive US government measures on Brazil designed to weaken Lula and boost the Bolsonaros, the 10 people told Reuters. The policies included designating Brazilian gangs as terrorist groups and imposing US sanctions against the Brazilian Supreme Court Justice who was spearheading the investigation into Jair Bolsonaro.

Reuters could not determine the extent to which the two men were acting on orders from the White House or Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Trump, a vocal defender of Bolsonaro since his election defeat in 2022, hasn’t publicly endorsed any candidate.

The White House declined to comment and referred questions to the State Department.

State Department Spokesman Tommy Pigott didn't answer questions about specific measures and directives involving Beattie and Pita but said in a statement: "All actions taken by the United States against narco-traffickers and to protect free speech are to defend the rights and lives of the American people. The Brazilian people have the right to choose their leaders through free and fair elections."

Lula’s office did not respond to comment requests.

Orna Blum, one of the officials who spoke to Reuters about Beattie and Pita’s efforts, led the State Department's Brazil and Southern Cone office until retiring last year over her opposition to the Trump administration.

Washington "has every right to pursue its economic and strategic interests," she said. "But when American foreign policy instruments are used to pressure another democracy over the legal fate of a political ally, the line between diplomacy and political intervention has been crossed."

SANCTIONS ON A SUPREME COURT JUSTICE

Beattie is a former White House speechwriter fired in 2018 after addressing an event frequented by white nationalists. He’s also the architect of "free speech diplomacy, opens new tab," a policy advocated by Trump allies that seeks to punish nations they accuse of censoring right-wing speech by US citizens, companies and global right-wing allies.

The United States has accused Brazil Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes of violating free speech rights by jailing Brazilians for political social-media posts and by censoring content of US social-media companies. Moraes has argued he was ridding social media of fake news that undermined public faith in Brazil's democratic institutions.

Moraes did not respond to a comment request.

Pita, a conservative Venezuelan-American, is among many in Rubio's orbit who view Lula as a threat to US interests in Latin America. Rubio has been a key leader in the administration’s aggressive policy in the region, which has included an invasion of Venezuela to oust its president, an oil blockade of Cuba, and military attacks on suspected drug boats from Latin America.

Beattie and Pita were drawn to the Bolsonaro family’s right-wing politics, their antipathy towards Lula, and the idea that Jair Bolsonaro was a victim of abuses by Brazil's Supreme Court.

Like Trump in the 2020 US election, Bolsonaro refused to concede he lost Brazil’s 2022 presidential vote, triggering riots by supporters who stormed government buildings. The Supreme Court convicted him in September 2025 of plotting a coup to remain in power.

Before the conviction, in early 2025, the Bolsonaros were aggressively lobbying Washington for sanctions under the Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act against Moraes, who had led criminal investigations into Jair Bolsonaro. The act is a 2016 federal law allowing US sanctions against foreign individuals responsible for human-rights abuses or severe corruption.

Around April 2025, Jair Bolsonaro’s younger son, Eduardo, visited Beattie in his State Department office in Washington DC, according to two former US officials. Eduardo Bolsonaro had been making the public case for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes since at least 2024, and in March 2025 he said in a livestream that it was "practically certain" the Trump administration would do so.

Eduardo Bolsonaro did not respond to requests for comment.

Beattie made calls to the US Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control to appeal for Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes, said a former US official with direct knowledge of the matter.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, whose department administers Magnitsky sanctions through OFAC, offered no opposition, the former official said.

The US announced Magnitsky sanctions against Moraes in July 2025, citing his alleged violations of free-speech rights by censoring anti-government social-media posts.

A Treasury official said Bessent and Rubio are "fully aligned on the administration’s foreign policy."

TERRORIST DESIGNATIONS

The Bolsonaro family was also pushing for Washington to designate Brazil's top gangs – the Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) – as terrorist organizations. They believed such a designation would hurt Lula, who some opponents have criticized for failing to control crime.

Eduardo Bolsonaro had become friends with Pita through US conservative circles, and both supported the effort to designate the gangs as terrorist groups.

In May 2025, Pita joined a US delegation, opens new tab that visited Jair Bolsonaro at his residence in Brasilia as he awaited his trial, according to public announcements at the time. Also in the group: David Gamble, the State Department’s top sanctions official at the time.

Back in Washington, Pita asked State sanctions officials to explore how terrorist designations like those announced against Mexican cartels in February 2025 could be used in Brazil, one former official said.

Nearly a year later, in May 2026 – after Pita was promoted to a new job that pulled him out of Brazil affairs – presidential contender Flavio Bolsonaro met with Beattie and Deputy Secretary of State Christopher Landau in Washington to discuss "the urgency of designating the PCC and the Comando Vermelho as foreign terrorist organizations," according to an X post by right-wing influencer Paulo Figueiredo that included photos of the attendees.

The State Department announced the designation, opens new tab the following day.

Reuters could not determine the extent of Pita or Beattie’s influence in securing the final decision.

BACKFIRES AND SETBACKS

In July 2025, Washington also announced a series of other measures against Brazil, including the revocations of eight Supreme Court justices' visas and 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods, citing the "persecution" of Jair Bolsonaro.

Reuters could not determine what, if any, role Beattie or Pita played in the additional measures. But if they were intended to undermine Lula, many of them backfired, according to political analysts in Brazil.

Measures targeting the court did nothing to stop it from proceeding with Bolsonaro's trial, while the tariffs boosted the Lula government's poll numbers, the analysts said.

Major US and Brazilian firms reliant on bilateral trade – including meatpacking giant JBS (JBSS.O), opens new tab - controlled by Brazilian billionaires Wesley and Joesley Batista – also pushed back on the tariffs, which Washington eventually watered down.

Beattie and Pita’s campaign also hit setbacks. Without an official explanation from the Treasury Department, the US removed Justice Moraes from the Magnitsky sanctions list in December, and in March Brazil barred Beattie from entering the country to visit Bolsonaro in prison.

Mario Braga, a Latin America analyst at risk intelligence firm RANE, said Trump may have decided to withhold a public endorsement of Bolsonaro to avoid being seen as meddling in Brazil's election – a perception that could boost Lula’s popularity.

Still, after Flavio Bolsonaro narrowly outperformed Lula in the first-round election earlier this month, Trump called it a big victory.

"Close, but a very, very big victory," he told reporters. "Amazing, actually."

items.title: Canada reports limited progress in trade talks with US
items.content_html:
OTTAWA, Oct 28 (Reuters) - There has been limited progress in trade talks with the United States to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, a Canadian government official with knowledge of the discussions said on Wednesday.

US President Donald Trump widened a trade rift by imposing 50% tariffs on a wide range of imports from Canada in August, accusing the US neighbor to the north of discriminatory treatment of American goods. Canada responded with retaliatory tariffs.

Reuters reported on Monday that the two countries were working on a trade deal. Talks on a broader agreement stalled in August when Canada walked away from the negotiating table.

"While discussions have continued, there has been limited progress," the Canadian official told Reuters, speaking on condition of anonymity.

Prime Minister Mark Carney, who on Monday said there had been "a slight intensification" in talks, reiterated on Wednesday that Canada is ready to sign an agreement that is in the interests of both nations.

"If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them, but we're not at that position right now," Carney told reporters.

A US government official said on Wednesday there were significant ongoing talks, including between US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Dominic LeBlanc, Canada's minister responsible for trade with the United States.

The White House said the Office of the US Trade Representative and the Commerce Department are continuing to work together on key issues involving trade with Canada, and that both Lutnick and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer have had discussions with their Canadian counterparts in recent days.

Trump's Republican Party is fighting to retain control of the US Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. Tariffs on Canadian imports have become a for the US president, with Republican candidates in border states calling for an end to the trade war with Canada.

Some experts have said the Trump administration may be less willing to make trade concessions to Canada after the midterms.

The latest talks have focused on tariffs imposed under Section 232 of US trade law, including up to a 50% tariff on Canadian steel and a 25% tariff on autos. The Commerce Department, which administers the Section 232 tariffs, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Trump on Sunday said the trade dispute would be resolved "soon," without providing specifics.

Trump signed an order last week to remove 50% tariffs on some Canadian agricultural and forestry products in a move that could benefit companies from Maine, where incumbent Republican Senator Susan Collins is locked in a tight reelection race. Trump added a number of Canadian products to the 50% tariff list to offset the tariff relief provided in his order.

items.title: US closes $5.1 billion loan to Alliant Energy for new gas power generation, energy storage
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 28 (Reuters) - The US Department of Energy said on Wednesday it has closed a $5.1 billion loan package to Alliant Energy (LNT.O), opens new tab to expand power generation and bolster the grid at plants in Iowa and Wisconsin.

The 30-year loans will support new natural gas-fired power plants, systems to store energy using batteries, and upgrades to existing generation facilities, it said. They will also create hundreds of construction-related jobs and deliver more than 2.6 gigawatts of new or upgraded power generation capacity, it said. That's enough power for nearly 1.8 million homes.

Lisa Barton, president and CEO of Alliant, said in a statement that the financing helps lower the cost of building power generation capacity and infrastructure while strengthening the grid and supporting long-term savings. Alliant, based in Wisconsin, said it projects that over the lifetime of the loans, customers would save up to $1.2 billion in power bills.

The loan had originally been proposed by the administration of former President Joe Biden, in his last days in office in January 2025, when it was only a conditional loan of $3 billion.

The office of Energy Dominance Financing, called the Loan Programs Office under Biden, has hundreds of billions of dollars in financing available, the bulk of which Energy Secretary Chris Wright has said will support nuclear power.

More than the name of the office has changed. Its mission during the Biden administration was to provide support to emerging clean energy projects and alternative vehicles that struggled to get bank loans. Now it includes support to projects such as natural gas that have typically been able to get bank loans. Energy storage, which typically includes batteries, was supported in both the initial and the closed loan.

"By bringing new, dependable power online, we are strengthening our nation’s energy security and lowering electricity costs for families and businesses across Iowa and Wisconsin," the loan office director, Gregory Beard, said in a release.

Any lowering of electricity costs could take many years as the loans take place over decades.

items.title: US Supreme Court denies immigration judges the power to shelve deportation cases
items.content_html:
Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US Supreme Court declined on Tuesday to reinstate the authority of immigration judges to temporarily postpone deportation cases, keeping in place an agreement between President Donald Trump's administration and Republican-governed Texas that bars the once-common practice.

The justices denied an emergency request by three US cities including Baltimore and an immigrant legal advocacy group to halt for now the deal ending the practice, known as "administrative closure," while litigation continues in the dispute.

The Supreme Court's decision, issued as a brief, one-sentence order, did not offer any explanation, as is common when it handles emergency requests. None of the justices publicly dissented from the decision.

The administration and Texas filed the agreement in a federal court in Texas on June 22, the same day that the state sued to challenge the immigration court procedure. A federal judge swiftly approved the agreement on the same day.

Baltimore and the other litigants said the federal government improperly colluded with Texas to secure the rule's invalidation. In a statement, the litigants and the lawyers representing them from the liberal legal group Democracy Forward expressed disappointment in Tuesday's decision.

"Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country," they said in the statement.

"This dangerous abuse of the judicial process threatens the rule of law and sets a troubling precedent for dismantling federal policies without meaningful public participation or judicial scrutiny," they added.

Representatives from the Justice Department and the Texas attorney general's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Immigration judges relied on administrative closure for decades to clear certain deportation cases off their busy dockets, including when separate proceedings involving the same person are pending that could prevent removal, such as on a visa petition or an appeal of a criminal conviction.

Critics including Texas and the Trump administration have said administrative closure has allowed immigrants who lack legal status to remain indefinitely in the United States, acting in effect like an amnesty.

HUNDREDS OF THOUSANDS OF CASES

Administrative closure has been applied over the years in hundreds of thousands of deportation cases. Ending the practice is part of Trump's hardline approach toward immigrants.

In 2024, Biden's administration adopted a regulation that formally codified administrative closure procedures, concluding that it lets judges efficiently manage their caseloads and promote the fair treatment of immigrants. That regulation replaced a prior rule adopted in 2020 during Trump's first term in office that had been judicially blocked.

After Trump returned to office in 2025, the Justice Department office that oversees immigration courts, the Executive Office for Immigration Review, announced it would not defend the Biden rule against a legal challenge.

In a lawsuit, Texas argued that the rule lets immigration judges "effectively grant indefinite amnesty to aliens illegally present in this country."

Trump's administration and the state then jointly asked US District Judge Reed O'Connor in Wichita Falls, Texas, to approve an agreement declaring the Biden rule unlawful. O'Connor did so, blocking it permanently, nationwide.

Three municipalities — Baltimore, New Haven, Connecticut, and Columbus, Ohio — and the legal services provider, Centro Legal de la Raza, sought to intervene in the case to defend the rule, but O'Connor rejected their bid. The cities say they all have substantial immigrant populations.

The New Orleans-based 5th US Circuit Court of Appeals declined to put the agreement on hold pending an appeal of O'Connor's decision.

The cities and Centro Legal de la Raza told the Supreme Court in a filing that Trump's administration circumvented a federal law governing agency procedures by using "manufactured litigation" with "ideologically aligned" Texas to eliminate a regulation it disliked.

"The need for interim relief is underscored by the collusion that infected this suit from its inception," they wrote.

items.title: US military says it struck vessel in Eastern Pacific, killing five
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 27 (Reuters) - The US military said on Tuesday five people were killed in a strike on a vessel in the Eastern Pacific, the latest in a series of attacks that Washington says targets "narco-terrorists" but human rights experts condemn as extrajudicial killings.

  • The US Southern Command "executed a lethal, kinetic strike on a go-fast vessel operating along established narco-trafficking routes in the Eastern Pacific," it said on X
  • It cited what it called "confirmed intelligence" to allege the vessel was actively involved in drug trafficking, without providing more details
  • It said five people were killed, describing them as "narco-terrorists"
  • President Donald Trump's administration has said the vessels it has struck since September 2025 were transporting narcotics
  • US strikes on such vessels in the Caribbean and Eastern Pacific have killed more than 230 people
  • Human Rights Watch, Amnesty International and independent UN experts have called the strikes unlawful extrajudicial killings while the American Civil Liberties Union has cast assertions by Trump's administration against those it targets as "unsubstantiated, fear-mongering claims"

(This story has been refiled to change 'ships' to 'vessels' in paragraph 6.)

items.title: Trump approval rises from record low to 32% ahead of midterm election, Reuters Ipsos poll finds
items.content_html:
WASHINGTON, Oct 26 (Reuters) - US President Donald Trump's public approval rating inched higher to 32%, up a percentage point from last week's record low, ahead of the November 3 midterm elections that will decide which party controls Congress, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll completed on Monday.

Trump's fellow Republicans are fighting to retain the party's majorities in the House of Representatives and Senate.

The five-day nationwide poll also showed that registered voters broadly favored Democrats over Republicans by 47% to 36% when asked which party they would pick for Congress in what is known as a "generic ballot" question. Some 11% said they did not know who they would vote for if the election were held today.

That gap of 11 percentage points between Democrats and Republicans was 1 percentage point tighter than in a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on October 19. The latest poll additionally asked undecided voters which party they were leaning toward. Factoring in their responses, the national race appeared somewhat tighter, with Democrats leading by 9 percentage points, 50% to 41%.

For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his second term as president.

Generic ballot polls are national polls that provide an overall view of which party poll respondents would like to see in charge in Congress. While these polls provide a view of national public sentiment, they do not capture the nuances of the state-by-state and district-by-district contests that determine control of the Senate and House, contests in which Republicans hold some structural advantages.

STEEP SENATE CLIMB FOR DEMOCRATS

Political analysts generally see the Democrats having a good chance of winning control of the House, but think they face a steeper climb to win the Senate.

It remains to be seen how many voters will actually cast ballots. The voters who appeared most likely to vote still favored Democrats over Republicans by 9 points, 53% to 44%.

The fight for Congress has appeared to turn on views around inflation, which has surged since Trump ordered military strikes on Iran in February that sent gasoline prices higher. Some 73% of voters in the poll said their cost of living was heading in the wrong direction.

Prior to the start of the war, Reuters/Ipsos polls showed voters preferring Republicans over Democrats as the better stewards of the US economy. The latest poll showed 37% of voters said Democrats have a better approach on the economy, compared to 33% who picked Republicans on the issue.

The poll also suggested Democratic voters were more excited about voting, with 46% of Democrats saying they were very enthusiastic about the midterms, compared to 30% of Republicans who said the same.

The Reuters/Ipsos poll, which was conducted online, gathered responses from 1,679 US adults, including 1,280 registered voters, and had a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all adults and 3 points for registered voters.

items.title: Dollar General overcharged shoppers, FTC and states allege in lawsuit
items.content_html:
Oct 26 (Reuters) - Dollar General (DG.N), opens new tab repeatedly charged more than advertised prices even after receiving tens of thousands of consumer complaints, the US Federal Trade Commission and 20 states alleged in a lawsuit filed on Monday.

Dollar General, which appeals to low-income consumers with bargain prices, made millions of dollars by failing to honor prices advertised on fliers and shelves at checkout, the FTC and states allege.

The discount retailer's stock was down more than 4% on Monday afternoon.

"Dollar General has, for years, repeatedly mislabeled prices, overcharged consumers and failed to correct the issue despite extensive corporate knowledge of the problem," the FTC and states said in a statement.

Representatives for Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The lawsuit cited numerous complaints from consumers, failed inspections conducted by state authorities, and undercover shopping sprees conducted by the FTC.

Portions of the lawsuit detailing the company's knowledge of the practices were largely redacted.

California joined the FTC lawsuit along with Florida, Illinois, Michigan, Ohio, North Carolina, Tennessee and 13 other states.

Since 2019, Dollar General has paid $6 million in settlements with six states over inaccurate pricing, according to the complaint.

items.title: US judge says he will rule Wednesday in lawsuit over California voter rolls
items.content_html:
Oct 27 (Reuters) - A federal judge said he would issue a ruling on Wednesday on the US Justice Department's emergency request to block California from counting mail ballots from alleged noncitizens.

US District Judge David Carter informed lawyers of his timeline at the end of a three-hour court hearing on Tuesday in Los Angeles.

items.title: US judge refuses to block Eli Lilly weight-loss drug ads, rules against Novo Nordisk
items.content_html:
Oct 26 (Reuters) - A US judge rejected on Monday Novo Nordisk's (NOVOb.CO), opens new tab request to block Eli Lilly (LLY.N), opens new tab from continuing advertisements for weight-loss drugs that the Danish drugmaker considered false and misleading, affecting markets with tens of billions of dollars of annual sales.

US District Judge Zahid Quraishi in Trenton, New Jersey, said Novo Nordisk did not deserve a preliminary injunction, having failed to show that Eli Lilly's ads threatened sales, undermined its goodwill, or caused lasting damage to its clinical reputation.

Quraishi called Novo Nordisk's claim of irreparable harm "inadequate to warrant the extraordinary relief it seeks." The judge ruled after a two-day hearing in late August.

Novo Nordisk sued Eli Lilly in July, saying ads for the obesity drug Zepbound and diabetes treatment Mounjaro violated federal and state false advertising and unfair competition laws by comparing higher doses of those products with lower doses of Novo Nordisk's Wegovy and Ozempic.

One commercial included a voiceover claim, with a written disclaimer, that people using Zepbound on average lost 50 pounds (23 kg) while people using Wegovy on average lost 33 pounds (15 kg).

"While we are disappointed with the court’s decision, today's ruling did not decide the question of whether Lilly's advertising is false and misleading, and this litigation is still ongoing," a Novo Nordisk spokesperson said in an email. "Everyone deserves clear, accurate and up-to-date information when making decisions about their health."

Eli Lilly, based in Indianapolis, has denied wrongdoing and said it was pleased with the decision.

WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS ARE BIG BUSINESS

Weight-loss drugs have become major businesses for large pharmaceutical companies. The United States is among a handful of countries that allow direct-to-consumer advertising of prescription medicines.

In his 25-page decision, Quraishi said that while Novo Nordisk's witnesses were credible, Eli Lilly's ads had at most a negligible market impact between April and July, with prescriptions for Novo Nordisk's products remaining stable.

The judge said money damages could compensate Novo Nordisk for any "nontrivial harm" it might suffer absent an injunction.

Quraishi also found Novo Nordisk's case "less than persuasive" based on a "very preliminary record," though he did not rule on the merits.

Novo Nordisk reported combined sales of about $32 billion for obesity medicines and Ozempic in 2025, court papers show.

The drugmaker is working to regain market share in the United States for its injectable obesity drugs, a market projected to exceed $100 billion by the end of the decade.
